# Memory and Matching: Detectors, Error Models, and the Clifford Proxy {#sec-matching}

::: {.callout-note title="🎯 Learning Goals"}
By the end of this chapter you can:

1. Read a STAR circuit as three phases — post-selected injection, decoded
   memory, perfect read-out — and say which detectors belong to which.
2. Explain what a detector error model is, and why minimum-weight matching
   needs it *decomposed* into edges.
3. Argue, at a whiteboard, why decoding a non-Clifford STAR circuit with
   the error model of its $\theta = 0$ Clifford proxy is exact for every
   error the decoder is responsible for.
4. Put a 95% Wilson interval on a rare-event rate, and say why the
   textbook normal interval fails exactly where this book needs it.
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
import math
import pathlib
import sys

import numpy as np

_here = pathlib.Path.cwd()
sys.path.insert(0, str(next(p for p in (_here, *_here.parents)
                            if (p / "starlab").is_dir())))
import starlab
from starlab.sampling import matcher
```

## Three phases in one file

Every published STAR circuit has the same shape, and it is worth being
able to sketch it from memory:

1. **Injection, post-selected.** Prepare the patch, run one round of
   syndrome extraction, apply the $k = d$ physical rotations, run two more
   rounds. That is three rounds of $d^2 - 1$ detectors each, and an attempt
   is kept only if all $3(d^2 - 1)$ of them read 0.
2. **Memory, decoded.** Run $d$ further rounds. Faults here are not
   discarded; they are *corrected*, by a decoder that reads the detectors
   and guesses whether the logical observable was flipped.
3. **Read-out, perfect.** Switch noise off, run one last clean round, undo
   the logical rotation exactly, and measure logical $X$. A 1 means the
   decoder's guess and reality disagree: a logical error.

The split matters because the two halves of the protocol answer to
different machinery. Post-selection handles everything before and during
the injection; the decoder handles only the memory.

```{python}
for d in (3, 5, 7):
    circ = starlab.star_circuit(d, 0.01)
    rounds = circ.num_detectors // (d * d - 1)
    print(f"d={d}: {circ.num_qubits:>3} qubits, {circ.num_detectors:>4} "
          f"detectors = {rounds} rounds x {d * d - 1}; post-select "
          f"the first {starlab.n_postselected(d)}")
```

The round count is $3 + d + 1$ every time: three injection rounds, $d$
memory rounds, one perfect round.

## Detectors and the error model

A **detector** is a parity of measurement outcomes that is deterministic
when nothing goes wrong — usually the same stabilizer measured in two
consecutive rounds. A fault anywhere in the circuit flips some set of
detectors and possibly the logical observable. Listing, for every possible
fault, *which* detectors and observables it flips and *how likely* it is,
gives the circuit's **detector error model** (DEM) [@gidney2021stim].

Minimum-weight perfect matching [@higgott2025sparse] works on a graph: each
fault must flip at most two detectors, so that it is an edge. A depolarizing
fault often flips more — a $Y$ error trips both $X$-type and $Z$-type
checks — and has to be *decomposed* into edges the decoder can use. stim
does that decomposition when asked.

## The obstacle, and the proxy

tsim [@haenel2026tsim] will produce a DEM for a STAR circuit, but it will
not decompose it: with non-Clifford rotations in the circuit, the logical
observable is not deterministic, and decomposition is only defined when it
is. So the decoder cannot be built from the true circuit directly.

The way out is in how tsim writes the rotations for stim. Each `R_Z(θ)`
becomes a stim identity gate carrying a tag, `I[R_Z(theta=…)]`; stim ignores
the tag. So `circuit.stim_circuit` *is the same circuit at θ = 0*: Clifford,
with a deterministic observable, decomposable.

::: {.callout-important .whiteboard title="🧑‍🏫 Whiteboard — Why the Clifford proxy decodes the memory exactly"}
**Claim.** For every Pauli fault after the physical rotations, the proxy
DEM records exactly the detectors and observable that fault flips in the
true circuit.

**Why.** After the rotation layer, the true circuit and the proxy contain
the same Clifford gates and measurements; they differ only by the logical
rotation applied to the encoded state, and by the perfect unrotation at
the end. A Pauli fault $P$ at some later point propagates through the same
Cliffords to the same Pauli on the measurements, so it flips the same
detectors in both. For the observable: the read-out undoes the logical
rotation exactly, so the logical $X$ measured at the end differs from the
noiseless outcome exactly when the accumulated logical Pauli
anticommutes with $X_L$ — the same condition as in the proxy.

**What it does not cover.** Faults *before or during* the rotations do not
merely propagate: an $X$ fault before $R_Z(\theta^*)$ turns it into
$R_Z(-\theta^*)$, which changes the injected angle. Those are not the
decoder's job. They are the post-selection's — and, when they slip through
it, they are exactly the injection errors this book measures.
:::

```{python}
for d in (3, 5):
    circ = starlab.star_circuit(d, 0.01)
    dem = circ.stim_circuit.detector_error_model(decompose_errors=True)
    m = matcher(circ)
    print(f"d={d}: {dem.num_errors:>4} error mechanisms, "
          f"{m.num_edges:>4} matching edges, "
          f"{m.num_detectors:>4} detectors in the graph")
```

The decomposition succeeds with no failures ignored: `matcher` builds the
model with stim's default, which raises if any fault cannot be split into
edges.

## A rate is a count, and a count needs an interval

Below threshold, logical errors are rare. A rate of $10^{-4}$ measured on
$10^6$ accepted shots is about a hundred events, and the uncertainty in it
is a property of that count, not of the shots. Every rate in this book is
printed with a 95% **Wilson score interval**, and the reason is the case
this book meets constantly: few or no failures.

::: {.callout-important .whiteboard title="🧑‍🏫 Whiteboard — The Wilson interval, and why not the normal one"}
**The normal interval** is $\hat p \pm z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$. At
$\hat p = 0$ it collapses to the single point 0 — it claims certainty from
zero observations of a rare event.

**Wilson** inverts the score test instead: find every $p$ for which
$|\hat p - p| \le z\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. Squaring gives a quadratic in $p$,
whose roots are
$$\frac{\hat p + \frac{z^2}{2n} \pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}
  + \frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n}} .$$

**At zero failures** this gives $[0,\; z^2/(n + z^2)]$ — about $3.84/n$ at
95%, close to the "rule of three". The interval stays inside $[0, 1]$ and
never claims more than the count supports.
:::

```{python}
for errors, shots in ((0, 10**6), (5, 10**6), (100, 10**6), (557, 811245)):
    lo, hi = starlab.wilson(errors, shots)
    print(f"{errors:>4} / {shots:>7}:  rate {errors / shots:.2e}   "
          f"95% [{lo:.2e}, {hi:.2e}]")
```

::: {.callout-tip .rosetta title="🔤 Vocabulary — The Words in Chapter 7"}
| What a paper says | What it is |
|---|---|
| *detector* | a parity of measurements that is deterministic without faults |
| *detector error model (DEM)* | every fault, with the detectors and observables it flips and its probability |
| *decomposition* | splitting a fault that flips many detectors into graph edges |
| *minimum-weight perfect matching* | pair up fired detectors by the most likely set of faults |
| *Clifford proxy* | the same circuit with every rotation set to zero |
| *Wilson interval* | the confidence interval from inverting the score test |
:::

   PyMatching?** What property of the circuit blocks it?
2. **Which faults does the Clifford proxy model exactly, and which does it
   not?** What handles the rest?
3. **You measured 0 failures in $10^6$ shots. What do you report?**

   one?** (Hint: a single round cannot tell a data error from a measurement
   error.)

::: {.callout-caution title="💪 Exercises"}
1. **Count the rounds.** From `star_d=7.stim`, verify that the detector
   count is $(3 + d + 1)(d^2 - 1)$ by counting `DETECTOR` lines.
2. **Wilson at the edge.** For $n = 10^6$, at how many observed errors does
   the Wilson interval's lower end first exceed zero by more than a factor
   of two below the point estimate?
3. **Proxy on a toy.** Build a three-qubit repetition code in stim with a
   tagged `I` in it, and show that the DEM is identical with and without
   the tag.
4. **Decomposition by hand.** Take one `DEPOLARIZE1` fault on a data qubit
   in the d = 3 circuit and list the detectors its $X$, $Y$ and $Z$
   components flip. Which component needs decomposing?
:::
